title: How Professionals Adapt to Artificial Intelligence: The Role of Intertwined Boundary Work
pub: Journal of Management Studies, vol. 62, no. 5, pp. 1991–2024; published online 31 May 2023, issue July 2025
author: James Faulconbridge · Atif Sarwar · Martin Spring

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Professional authority: AI enters an already contested field
st.an: The supplied excerpt provides no substantive argument, evidence or findings, so the source’s position on whether legal AI should be understood as a contest over expertise, legitimacy and institutional power cannot be determined.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI reallocates junior production and threatens the traditional staffing pyramid. It materially extends that proposition by identifying technologists as an increasingly central cohort whose roles may reshape partnership eligibility, professional career paths and firms’ service models, while retaining lawyers for interpretation, judgment and verification.
qs: Professionals do less manual data assembly and initial analysis work but take on new tasks associated with interpreting and acting on the outputs of AI systems.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core reconfiguration thesis and materially extends it by explaining how professionals strategically redefine occupational boundaries, create interpretive and advisory work, and reorganize firms around technologists. Its 2018–2020 evidence also supports the cluster’s caution that observed task reallocation had not yet produced mass professional displacement, while remaining provisional.
qs: This means that rather than spelling the ‘end of the professions’, AI is leading to reconfigured forms of professional activity, jurisdiction, and PSFs.

Moreover, PSFs are adapting, both through the redefinition of the services they provide to clients, and through the reorganization of systems of work and governance to accommodate a different role for professionals, alongside new actors such as technologists that enable the use of AI.

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that AI-driven change is shaped by professional agency and organisational arrangements, and materially develops it through the concept of intertwined boundary work. It shows how professionals selectively defend and expand jurisdiction while collaboration with technologists redistributes work and power within firms.
qs: By examining the adoption of AI in accounting and law professional service firms (PSFs), we show how professionals respond through intertwined boundary work, this being the process by which professionals respond to disruptions and protect interests and resources by engaging in multiple interdependent modes of boundary work.
Interdependencies between collaborative boundary work (negotiating) and configurational boundary work (coalescing) lead to changes to divisions of work and power structures in PSFs.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of selective automation and human-led work redesign, finding that professionals cede routine tasks while retaining interpretation and judgment. It materially extends the proposition by explaining redesign as intertwined boundary work that also creates advisory services, integrates technologists and changes partnership governance.
qs: Professionals do less manual data assembly and initial analysis work but take on new tasks associated with interpreting and acting on the outputs of AI systems.

Moreover, PSFs are adapting, both through the redefinition of the services they provide to clients, and through the reorganization of systems of work and governance to accommodate a different role for professionals, alongside new actors such as technologists that enable the use of AI.

st.t: Legal prediction: Classification cannot guarantee sound advice
st.an: The source broadly supports bounded, human–machine decision support: it presents predictive analytics as informing judgments about case selection, strategy, fees and charging rather than independently guaranteeing sound legal advice. It also reinforces the cluster’s organisational point that predictive work requires data-analysis expertise and expands decision-making beyond lawyers, although the excerpt supplies no performance evidence establishing practical reliability.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on translating technical capability into redesigned professional workflows and multidisciplinary delivery, showing electronic investigation focusing human analysis and predictive tools bringing data specialists into legal decision-making. Its support is limited by the absence of task-specific accuracy, reliability or outcome evidence.

kp.k: Evidence concerns English firms adopting AI during 2018–2020
kp.d: Faulconbridge, Sarwar and Spring examine accounting and law professional service firms serving corporate clients in England, with revenues of £25–250 million. Research conducted between 2018 and 2020 combined 876 reports and articles, 34 scoping interviews and 51 subsequent interviews: 25 in accounting firms and 26 in law firms. Firms were selected for relatively advanced AI use or ongoing implementation projects. The study elaborates theory through interviews supported by documentary analysis; its empirical period precedes the ChatGPT example used in the introduction. The article was published online on 31 May 2023 and assigned to the July 2025 issue.
qs: We conducted research between 2018 and 2020
using documentary materials (876 reports and articles) and 34 scoping interviews with representatives of accounting and law firms and technology providers.
The second stage involved a series of 51 interviews with key actors in accounting and law firms with ongoing AI implementation projects.

kp.k: Professional adaptation combines four interdependent forms of boundary work
kp.d: The authors identify defending existing jurisdiction, creating new domains, negotiating collaboration and coalescing organizational spaces. Their central theoretical contribution is that these responses are interdependent rather than simply simultaneous: opportunity ties allow one response to enable additional benefits, necessity ties make one response depend on others, and recursive reinforcement consolidates earlier changes. Professional protection can therefore involve both strengthening exclusion around some activities and weakening boundaries around others.
qs: multiple interdependent modes of boundary work
opportunity ties, when one mode of boundary work creates an opportunity for other modes that generate additional benefits for the group in question;
necessity ties, when one mode of boundary work necessitates other modes because of ripple effects that make the success of the first mode contingent on the enactment of other modes.
recursive change reinforcement, defined here as when one mechanism of change consolidates another.

kp.k: Professionals relinquish routine work while defending human judgement
kp.d: Interviewees accepted AI and technologists taking over initial data collation and review, including tasks previously performed by junior accountants and lawyers. They simultaneously restated claims to distinctive expertise in contextual interpretation, ambiguity, judgement and client advice. The authors interpret this as strategic boundary defence, not merely technological substitution. Claims that machines cannot exercise professional judgement are participants' assertions supporting professional jurisdiction, rather than independently established limits on AI capability.
qs: Defending involved focusing on what AI could not do, rather than focusing on what it could do.
there’s an element of the professional judgement call that no machine can ever do
it’s basically admin, it’s not being a lawyer
It’s all about getting to the information or to the decision quicker and then the lawyer doing the sense check over it

kp.k: AI shifts junior tasks toward interpreting machine outputs
kp.d: The paper describes AI undertaking document review in law and transaction analysis in accounting that juniors previously completed manually. Professionals increasingly interpret and act on outputs rather than assemble the underlying data. Table II identifies a continuing junior role in first interpretation, alongside new career paths for technologists. These are qualitative accounts of task redistribution, not quantified estimates of junior job losses or evidence about the long-term effectiveness of revised professional training.
qs: Previously, junior lawyers would have been tasked to review documents man- ually, using pen and paper or word processing/PDF software.
Professionals do less manual data assembly and initial analysis work but take on new tasks associated with interpreting and acting on the outputs of AI systems.

kp.k: Larger-scale analysis enables new advisory services
kp.d: AI makes previously costly or impractical dataset reviews feasible, allowing firms to expand their advisory domains. Accounting examples include reviewing one hundred percent of transactions and advising on operational patterns. Legal examples include reviewing entire supplier-contract portfolios for risks or renegotiation opportunities, and using employment-dispute data to sell preventive client training. The authors connect this expansion to earlier acceptance of AI-assisted analysis. An accounting partner's expectation that consultancy would become more valuable while compliance became less valuable is a forecast, not a measured pricing result.
qs: can do work that we never would have been able to do
the ability to review one hun- dred percent of a firm’s financial transactions, rather than a sample, generated new opportunities.
We have a training advisory service which we’ve built which also allows us to charge clients for training
I think the compliance piece will be devalued and the consultancy piece will be valued at a far higher figure

kp.k: Technologists become essential collaborators rather than peripheral support
kp.d: Firms developed specialist teams to configure and operate AI and provide analytical outputs to professionals. Technologists sometimes had legal or accounting training but could instead have data-analysis or computing expertise; they rarely held live practising certificates or direct responsibility for advisory billings. Their expertise became necessary to both protect existing professional work and deliver new services, legitimating access to activities previously reserved for qualified professionals. This included attendance at client meetings to explain how technology would add value.
qs: a dedicated team whose only job is to use Kira [an AI system], that’s it, putting the documents in, and then the output’s given to the lawyers
They rarely held live practising certificates and did not have direct responsibility for client advisory work and, in turn, billings.
being able to use technology well and being creative in how they can use technology
invited to client relationship meetings

kp.k: Partnership access expands to accommodate technical expertise
kp.d: Senior leaders in the studied firms had changed, or were changing, partnership-entry conditions to include technologists, legal process managers and operating officers. Mechanisms ranged from formal partnership admission to titles such as Principal that granted decision-making input where legal structures constrained formal membership. The authors interpret these changes as necessary to sustain collaboration with strategically important specialists. They report flatter structures and challenges to traditional status hierarchies, but do not establish a measured change in associate-to-partner leverage.
qs: senior and managing partners had or were in the process of changing the conditions for entry into the partnership
full amendments allowing formal partnership status
titles such as Principal which signified the right to input into partnership decision-­making
What this firm has done is turn the model on its head and put the tech people at the top of the pyramid and put the accountants lower down

kp.k: AI implementation redistributes managerial authority over professional work
kp.d: Technologists' strategic importance gave them greater authority to standardize data, train professionals and challenge established work practices. The authors regard this as consequential because professional partnerships traditionally reserved legitimate control over work methods and quality standards to qualified professionals. Changes could be controversial and generally required partner approval, but partners accepted them because they supported protected professional work and new services. Client demands for implementation plans and accountable project management reinforced this shift.
qs: data interpretation is only as good as the data that’s actually in the system, so you have to have a robust process of getting source documentation into the system
why are you deviating from the protocols supplied in the last 30 cases?
Changes to partnerships and management control to enable greater input from technologists ultimately required the consent of partners, who usually had to approve the changes through a vote.

kp.k: Collaborators gain strategic roles, not merely discarded routine work
kp.d: Against prior research emphasizing professionals passing lower-skilled work to subordinate groups, the authors find that technologists also produce strategically important insights enabling professionals to expand their domains. Their role in protecting incumbent interests supports their own access to governance and management. The resulting relationship is therefore not simply one in which lawyers retain power while delegating unwanted tasks; professional protection and increased collaborator influence can develop together.
qs: technologists responsible for AI systems completed initial analysis but also delivered new insights that assisted accountants’ and lawyers’ creation boundary work.
the heightened strategic importance of collaborators such as technologists

kp.k: Observed adaptation complicates predictions of professional extinction
kp.d: The authors conclude that AI automates some tasks while professionals actively redefine and potentially expand their work, and firms reorganize services and governance. They report that these responses were not producing mass redundancies at the time studied. This is a qualified conclusion about observed adaptation, not proof that displacement will never occur or that all firms will preserve employment.
qs: Professionals are redefining their roles and work in ways that, at the moment at least, are not leading to mass redundancies.
the responses also exploit the opportunities that AI creates to redefine and where possible expand the domain of professionals
The effects of AI will continue to evolve

kp.k: Generalizability and conditions for intertwined adaptation remain uncertain
kp.d: The authors caution that findings may depend on professional closure, regulatory context, organizational culture and leadership. They call for testing in other professions and organizational settings, including consulting and healthcare. Some firms might respond purely defensively; less severe disruptions might not trigger intertwined responses. They also leave open whether defence must occur first and whether opportunity and necessity ties must coexist. These are research questions rather than established findings.
qs: Boundaries that protect resources and interests like those found in account- ing and law PSFs do not exist in all occupational contexts
different organizational cultures and forms of leadership could result in responses to AI that are purely defen- sive
it is important to consider whether opportunity and necessity ties always emerge together as part of intertwined boundary work, or whether intertwining can result from just one of the two ties.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors find that AI reconfigures professional tasks, services and governance rather than simply replacing accountants and lawyers.
pts.d: The authors describe several connected changes. AI takes over some initial data assembly, document review and analysis previously undertaken by junior professionals, while lawyers and accountants retain interpretation, contextual judgement and advice. Professionals defend this division by relinquishing claims over routine work and restating claims to distinctive human expertise; interviewed professionals' assertions that machines cannot exercise professional judgement are boundary-defending claims, not demonstrated technical limits. AI also makes previously uneconomic analysis feasible, enabling new advisory services: reviewing clients' supplier contracts for risk or renegotiation opportunities; analysing employment disputes to sell preventive training; and reviewing accounting transactions comprehensively to advise on working practices. Delivering these services requires technologists, data specialists and project managers, whose roles extend beyond subordinate support to client meetings, strategic contributions, partnership participation and managerial authority. The authors explain these changes through intertwined boundary work: defending existing professional domains creates opportunities to expand into new domains, while dependence on technologists necessitates collaboration and changes to governance. They conclude that new types of professional work replace some work transferred to AI, without claiming that all displaced tasks or jobs are quantitatively offset. Table II additionally describes faster contract review and generation, broader electronic discovery, and predictive analysis informing case acceptance, fees and litigation strategy; these are presented as tool-category impacts rather than separately measured outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is a qualitative study of AI adoption, combining interviews and documentary analysis rather than performance benchmarks or employment statistics.
pts.d: Faulconbridge, Sarwar and Spring conducted research during 2018–2020. Stage one comprised 34 scoping interviews: 15 in accounting and 19 in law, including technology providers. Documentary analysis covered 876 materials: 587 Accounting Today articles, 271 Legal Week articles and 18 reports from professional bodies, consultants and firms. Stage two comprised 51 interviews, including 25 in accounting firms and 26 in law firms, with partners, practising professionals, technologists and operational leaders. The researchers selected comparatively advanced AI adopters and firms with ongoing implementation projects, used manifest and latent coding, and developed a theoretical account of interconnected boundary changes. Concrete interview examples include dedicated Kira teams supplying outputs to lawyers, a paid training service based on employment-dispute patterns, technologists joining client meetings, and technology specialists entering partnership or exercising managerial influence. Table II draws on interviews and industry reports. Predictions about universal lawyer-plus-AI superiority, consultancy becoming more valuable, or machines never making professional judgement calls belong to the interviewed speakers. The paper does not supply controlled productivity or accuracy comparisons, measured litigation improvements, or a quantitative test of employment displacement; its conclusion about the absence of mass redundancies is a qualified qualitative interpretation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Findings concern adoption in 2018–2020, with explicitly provisional conclusions about employment and future professional survival.
pts.d: Although published online in 2023 and assigned to a 2025 issue, the empirical study concerns 2018–2020. The introductory reference to ChatGPT and Allen & Overy is later contextual material, not evidence that the interview findings measure contemporary generative AI. The authors' conclusion that professional adaptation is not producing mass redundancies is qualified by 'at the moment at least'; they give no long-term displacement forecast. Advisory expansion depends on AI making large datasets economical to review and on professionals combining resulting insights with their expertise. Collaboration and governance changes depend on technologists' skills, usable data, standardised processes, managerial sponsorship and partner consent. Some partnership changes were completed while others were underway. The authors distinguish legal structures that permit formal non-lawyer partnership participation from arrangements requiring alternative titles or informal decision-making access. They explicitly leave generalisation to other professions, organizational settings and firms unresolved, suggesting that culture, leadership, regulatory context and disruption severity may alter responses. Their prediction of continuing organizational effects is directional, without a deadline or quantified magnitude.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are English mid-sized corporate-service law and accounting firms, their professionals and technology specialists, and their business clients.
pts.d: The empirical setting is mid-sized professional service firms in England with revenues of £25–250 million serving corporate clients. Junior lawyers and accountants lose some manual review and data-assembly tasks and take on interpretation of AI outputs; senior professionals seek to retain judgement-intensive work and expand advisory roles. Technologists, who may or may not have legal or accounting training and rarely hold live practising certificates, gain access to professional workflows, client meetings, senior decision-making and sometimes partnership. Existing partners retain distinctive professional roles but accept some constraints on autonomy as technologists and process managers influence data practices and work organization. Corporate clients receive broader analysis, preventive advice and training that had previously been too costly to purchase. The authors suggest that AI helps firms outside the largest accounting and legal practices expand advisory offerings despite limited human research capacity. Consultants and organizational-development specialists are potential competitors in those expanded domains, although the authors report little competition arising during the study. These are enterprise-service and organizational findings, not evidence about unmet civil legal need, consumer access to justice, ALSP market share or profession-wide staffing reductions. References to flatter structures concern hierarchy and authority; the study does not establish a measured change in associate-to-partner leverage.
